title: Integrating Generative AI Into Business Strategy: Dr. George Westerman
transcript: TODD GLICKMAN: But now, I'm very pleased to introduce Dr. George Westerman, Principal Research Scientist at the MIT Sloan School of Management. Dr. Westerman is a world-recognized thought leader in leading transformation and competitive advantage through technological innovation. He works at the really exciting intersection of executive leadership and digital innovation to provide continuous, valuable insights to leaders in all industries. George, welcome. GEORGE WESTERMAN: Thanks, Todd. It's really great to be here. And it's especially great because at home, we got 5 inches of snow yesterday. And there was no snow on the ground here. So that's a good thing. So yeah, I teach in the management school. And so what I focus on-- he said technology, innovation, and leadership. I try to take technologies and make them-- to demystify them, to help leaders understand what's happening there and really think about how do you design your organization and how do you lead transformation? So I did some of the earliest research on digital transformation 15 years ago. To tell you how long ago that was, nobody used the word digital transformation back then. And so I wrote some book on that. I had done a work with IT organizations before that. I've done work in skills and careers. And now, of course, AI, all of those things come together. AI is affecting all of that. And so what I want to do today is talk to you a little bit about how do you think about generative AI and how do you work that in your strategy? Now, Eric has been doing AI for almost as long as I've been alive. And I want to try to tell you about AI from a management standpoint. And that means it will-- I'll try to make it crystal clear for you in trying to make decisions in your organization. But it also means that if Eric and I disagree, he's correct. So that's where we want to go. My job is to be as clear as possible, help you figure out the questions you can ask, the instincts to develop, as you are making decisions, because all of you, probably, are having to make decisions with AI. How can AI help you understand that a little bit better? Or if I could say it a different way, how can I make it a little bit less scary and make you feel more competent in dealing with this stuff? So are you ready to go? Three pieces here-- number one is, what is AI? Now, Eric already talked about what is AI. I'm going to give you my version of it. And think about these elements of the different kinds of AI and how to think about it. Number two is GenAI because that's really where we're spending a lot of time now, a lot of attention on ChatGPT, and Gemini, and Midjourney, and all these, Sora, and all these others. How do you think about making that work in your organization? Because it's tremendously powerful, but also very risky. And how do you think about that? And then the last is, what does that mean? How are companies innovating with this right now? So first, what is AI? And like I said, it's a little bit scary, after having followed an AI professor. But like I said, it's mostly correct and hopefully very clear when we talk about it. What is AI? Well, the thing about what is AI is, it's really hard. The definitions Eric gave were from 2003. Now, Google does not track Google Trends back in 2003. They start in 2004. And look at generative AI. Nobody was talking about it because it didn't exist back then. But then deep learning, he talked about that, and you could see how that came on 10 years ago or something like that. That was really cool. We had a thing called the Work of the Future Initiative. And the question there was, with deep learning doing what it is doing, what jobs will be left after the robots eat the jobs? And we found that, actually, they don't eat the jobs. They eat pieces of the jobs. And also, there's a lot of extra effort that goes in. It's not just the technology. But that was the scariest, most interesting AI. And now, what do we call that? We call that traditional AI. That's how fast these things move. Go back a little bit farther, this is machine learning. And you can see, why is it bigger? Well, it's actually a superset of these other two and then artificial intelligence. And the interesting thing about this, you see, artificial intelligence was more common. And now, it's less common because artificial intelligence back then was a different kind of thing than it is now, just like Eric was talking about. So with these elements, how do you make sense out of this mess when it keeps moving so quickly? I'm going to really first give you my important law that if you remember nothing else, remember this. You know Moore's law, Moore's law and the exponential. These things keep growing at an exponential rate. This is Westerman's law. Westerman's law is different. Technology changes quickly. Organizations change much more slowly. I know this to be true. I should not have to say this is true. But I know it to be true. And you know it to be true. But our technology people often forget this. And your technology vendors often forget this. The hard part is not adopting the technology. It's changing the way you do business. It's not the digital. It's the transformation, is the hard part. And so what does that mean? Technology is not the problem. Transformation is. So it's not really a technical problem. It's also very much a leadership problem. We need to get both of those things in there. And so, for example, in talking about AI, we've talked to two-- we've talked to a lot of executives. But here's two that we can quote. Matthew Evans, who worked on AI for the manufacturing process at Airbus, he says, "Strictly speaking, we don't invest in AI or natural language processing or image. We are always investing in a business problem." Or if we go on to the Home Depot, Fahim Siddiqui-- another thing I do is I run the MIT Sloan CIO Leadership Award every year. And Fahim was one of our finalists last year. And Home Depot is a home goods store. If you need hardware, or saws, or wood, or anything, you go to Home Depot. I'm renovating a house right now, so I spent a lot of time in Home Depot. And Fahim and his team have created a really good experience for a really, really complicated store. He says, we should always be looking for extraordinary experiences We want to bring joy to the user. We want to delight. The technology-- that's secondary. And once again, we forget that all the time. But we can't forget that because technology provides zero value to your company. What you do with the technology is what creates that value, how you change your business or your products to make it work better. So what's the first thing from a management side? What's the first thing you need to know about AI? Artificial intelligence is not intelligent. And Eric mentioned this, and we should continue that. Basically, it's a program that executes, but it doesn't have that context knowledge. And we have to remember that. It's basically executing a formula. And that formula is what you've programmed it to do, what it's learned how to do. But it may not be the right thing. Aude Oliva, who has created AI that can actually read what you are thinking, with brain scans, one of the smartest people I know, she says, artificial intelligence should be artificial idiots. That's one way to think about this. It's not intelligent. But the thing is, it can act very intelligently. And that's very useful, as long as we are careful, as long as we do it in the right way. So the digital transformation research-- this is an update. We started this in 2010. This is an update from 2021. Where can you look for opportunities not from AI, not just from AI, but from mobile, and from Internet of Things, and from other technologies you're facing? Four good areas you can look-- one is creating an emotionally engaging, targeted, personalized customer experience, number one. Number two is operations, not just automation, but the ability to adapt and adjust as things go on. That's industry 4.0. Business models-- not just being the Alibaba or the Amazon of your industry, but what can you do with information to make more low-hanging fruit, turning your products into services, these kinds of things? And what we rediscovered-- we should have noted before-- employee experience. Employee experience is a critical part. We know that satisfied employees lead to satisfied customers. We also know that if you have a bad employee experience, it's a very good indication that your systems and your processes are not running the way they should or your incentives. So when you're looking for what to do with AI, it's the same way we think about any other digital transformation work. You can look in these areas, and not only in these areas, but the opportunity to go across, like Home Depot has done, like Airbus has done. You'll see also that this rides on top of your systems, your data, your systems. And if that's a mess, it's hard to do this. AI actually helps a little bit with that messy data. But the better your data is, the cleaner your processes are, the better you will be. So I really think of AI as the next stage of digital transformation. The same principles apply. But there's more that you can do. And there are more powerful opportunities. And so we still need to lead this, but we need to think more and more about what we can do. So here are some things we could do with generative AI. I have designed courses over time. We're doing one in the Philippines right now, a set of courses. And instead of me standing up, and putting a suit, on and going in front of a camera, now we just type words in, and she will say it instead. And if you don't like how she looks, somebody else that looks different will do it. And they can do it in a different language. And frankly, I can do it with a deepfake very easily. I don't need to go to a studio anymore. Also, any corporate literature you have can be in any language you want, instantly, with a push of a button. Over here, certainly coding-- many people are doing coding right now. How many of you are your programmers? Are they using Copilots and things like that? Well, if they are not, it's time to start. This really does help. Now, there are questions about whether it's better for the senior people or the junior people, but there's a learning process. And it is better. It's not only better for coding, but also enforcing standards and making documentation. People hate doing that. The computer can help them. What else is there? Well, Cresta. Cresta is a call center tool, especially for sales. And you heard some really good startups. In a randomized trial at MIT, they found that everybody using this tool got better. The most senior people got 14% better. The most junior people got 34% better. If you have the senior and the junior people, they raise the bar for everybody, and it moves up. What does it do? It listens to you talk and it gives you hints while you are talking. That person is getting confused. Explain the product better. That person is getting angry. Try this to calm them down. And then at the end, it comes back and says, looking across what you've been doing, you don't close fast enough. Try to get to the sale faster, these kinds of things. It becomes what a good supervisor would be. But it's with you all the time. And I'm working on a project right now with the media lab, where we are creating a personalized tutor for the programming class, the first Python class, for minority institutions, minority learning institutions. The idea is, if we can get people through that first class, with an individualized tutor, they are on a set for a career that they never would have had possible. But people drop out of that first class because they do not have a tutor. So we're developing that right now. And then last but not least, those of you who are using any products, whether it's SAP, or Workday, or Adobe, this is being integrated into all of your products. So this is happening all over the place. But once again, it's not the technology, it's what do you do with the technology that makes it better. The other thing that's really important here is we talk about generative AI solutions. But most of the best solutions are a combination of generative AI, traditional AI, boring old IT, and also people and process in there. So Lemonade, they have a very specific niche in the insurance market. They write 98% of their policies, 98% of first claim notices, and they handle 50% of claims automatically. Through this combination of different AIs and also traditional systems, what about that 50%? Well, the easy stuff, the computer does it. And the hard stuff, they give it to a person to figure out what to do. That's how their model works. And this is Sysco. This is not the technology company Cisco. This is Sysco, the food service delivery. They have one of the largest truck fleets in the world. Restaurants around the world get supplied by these. And here are all the different ways that Sysco is applying AI in what they do. Now, this is not a high tech company. They deliver cans of stuff to restaurants. But you can see all the different things they have on the customer experience side over there and also on the back office. And when Tom Peck, when I was talking with him about what he does, all those little brains, those are opportunities where generative AI can help. We think about generative AI in helping a salesperson figure out their call planning. But how about generative AI in helping you route things around a warehouse or a-- we don't have this thing they want. We don't have this kind of mushroom. But this kind of mushroom will work, so all kinds of opportunities there. So if you ask three AI experts, what are the categories of AI, you will get five different answers. Nobody can really agree. So I'm going to give you my four categories. And I'm not going to tell you this is right. I'm going to tell you it's mine, if that helps, so four categories. And this should look familiar because Eric talked about a lot of this. And what I want to do is walk you through these, just to give you a little bit more instinct on what to do about these things. So number one, rule-based systems-- Eric called it expert systems. Put a lot of if/then statements together. 1984, when I first started programming, one of my first jobs was to create an engine for a rule-based system. And like Eric said, these things don't work beyond the simplest problems. But now, rules engines are better and if you use them in the right environments, prescriptions, loan making these kinds of things. Within the limits in which they are good, they are useful. But don't try to get outside that context. Then there's econometrics, which is statistics. Most of us learned in school deep learning, generative AI. Let's walk through these things. So expert systems, we talked about this. How do you program them? You talk to an expert. And the expert tries to figure it out. But there's a nice paradox, which is that we know more than we can tell. Or as Eric said, your two-year-old understands physics but couldn't tell you how that works. And we have that problem all the time. But you have to talk to an expert. You don't need any data, the expert. The good thing is, they will give you a precise answer, and they will give you the same answer every time. But they do not adapt. You add a rule, things get a little tricky. So that's one thing. Econometrics, that's the next thing. That's statistics. Many of you have probably learned statistics. You've probably forgotten much of it. But we still use this all the time. If you have structured data, meaning data that you can put into a spreadsheet, usually numeric data, these things work. And they work really well. They're pretty cheap to program and especially the two-click things. How do we create a formula for those two dimensions that will help us to figure out, is it a blue thing or a green thing? And they tend to be-- there are false positives. There are false negatives. But they tend to be pretty good. The other is looking at the trend line, looking at the regression These things actually work remarkably well with numeric data and also things you can turn into numeric data, like is he going to buy my product based on what I do to him? You can also do multiple dimensions. Finding that trend line with two dimensions is easy. Try it with 100 dimensions. I have a team right now currently looking at 100 million CVs, resumes, and tracking people's careers through that 100 million resumes to try to figure out what is a more or less productive path. You're not going to do that by just looking at two dimensions. And then, of course, you don't have to just look at lines. But you do have to have an idea of what the functional form is that you're looking at. So it's often numeric. There are some things, but you can do this. It's relatively cheap. It works really well. You get precise answers. You get the same answer every time. But it has to be numeric data. Then you have deep learning. And Eric talked a lot about deep learning. This was the coolest thing ever 15 years ago. And it's still pretty darn cool. Now, the thing is, Eric also showed you there are 50 different versions of this. So I'm just going to give you one archetype. This picture-- do you know what that picture is? It's a neural net. But what this picture mostly is? It's a thing that people use to scare you. It's a complicated-looking thing. And there's a little bit of magic involved in there. So Eric explained this, but let me explain it also a little bit more. You're taking inputs. You're running them through a set of weighted averages and coming out with a prediction of multiple different states at the end. And it sounds very easy, but it gets beyond human capability really fast. You train it with labeled data. You need to know the truth. That's why every time you log in, it says prove you are human. Tell us where there is a car. Tell us where there's a bicycle. You are labeling data to train these things. Every time you get on social media and they do the de-aging challenge-- show us you and show us you 20 years ago-- you're creating labeled data of old and young people. You need that data. And then you do the-- the outputs are repeatable. But they are in no way explainable. Our smartest people are just starting to figure out how to make this explainable. And it's going to be a little while. But I'm going to give you an example now. At MIT-- I'm going to get a little complicated on you, but I promise, not too complicated. The good thing is, I'm going to try to take this scary picture and make it a little bit more real. Eric started. I'll try it. And after the two of us, hopefully, it will make sense. What are those? Anybody? They're numbers. Now, try to tell me, if we were to say features, loops and lines and these kinds of things, tell me the formula to look at the number 2. How would you create the rules to decide what is a number 2? Well, it has a little loop at the top. And it has a loop down here. And then the number goes down. That's how a two looks, except no loop there. And there the line is going across instead of going down. If you were to try to program this with a bunch of features, you would probably not get very far. But 35 lines of code, 25 to 35 lines of code can do this no problem at all by doing this kind of thing. What do you do? Well, first of all, you take these two-dimensional objects and you turn them into a one-dimensional set of numbers. So 28 by 28 image becomes 784 pixels. Now, what you have just done is you've thrown away all the relationships between what is on top of each other. You've thrown it away. And the algorithm doesn't care. And then you put the numbers in the left hand side, and you have random numbers here. And it spits out 10 estimates, 0 through 9, how likely is it that that is the number. And so you come through, and you get this. Well, we think maybe it's a 2, a 1. We think maybe it's a 2. Maybe it's a 7 and some stronger or less strong estimates. And then you go back and say, hey, it's really a 9. And you go back the other way, and you turn all the knobs to make it a little bit better. Now, if that bothers you, how much do you turn each knob, it should bother you because nobody knows how much you turn each knob. But we do know, if you do this 10,000 times, the knobs end up in the right place. So if it sounds like magic to you, it is magic. It's the magic of large numbers and good algorithms. And so if you're wildly uncomfortable, then you are like the rest of us. We are all wildly uncomfortable with this. But it does work. So you do that 10,000 times, and it gets there. Now, what does that mean? Well, that means you've got to have labeled data. You need to know what that number really is. You need to do the reinforcement over and over again. And you need to back chain to adjust those numbers. If your data is biased-- let's say we have only data on men, but not women. Well, then what happens when a woman comes in? Amazon found this out. They were reviewing resumes to try to figure out what resumes look like their best engineers. And they were routinely rejecting women. Why was that? None of their engineers were women. And women talk differently. By the way, if you were the captain of the women's swimming team, you would never get a job. None of the men that they trained it on were ever captain of the women's swimming team and also different use. So they had to go and fix that bias, same thing if you train on men versus women, children versus adults, different parts of the world. So you got to get rid of that. You got to test that bias. You also need to make sure you actually have some kind of accuracy in your data. So that's it, no more on the neural nets. Do you understand that picture? I could test you, and you would know how to say that now? Well, at least nobody can scare you anymore. So then generative AI continues. And as Eric said, what they do now, not only they're using a lot of these similar algorithms, but they're also inventing. And they're saying, given what you told me and everything I know, what's the next best word or pair of words to say? And then it says, once I have that, given everything you told me and everything I know, plus everything I just invented, what's the next best word? What's the next best word? And it can get things very right, as you've seen. It can also get them very wrong. I first did my bio with ChatGPT. And the bio was really good, expert on digital transformation and innovation strategy, author of four award winning books, blah, blah, blah. I loved it. I've only written three books. I don't know what that fourth book is. And it wouldn't tell me. So you want to be careful. But the interesting thing about that is-- well, I'll come back to that in a minute. It randomly generates next. So why do you get a different answer every time? Because it is random. It's meant to be that way. And you can use that. It creates new things. It doesn't just classify. It creates new. It can be used for good as bad. You can get some boring stuff. You can also get creative stuff. But you also get this, the hallucinations. My favorite is this. This lawyer prepared all of his court documents using ChatGPT. And unfortunately, some of the cases that he cited as precedent for what he's doing were not real. That made the judge very angry. So not only did he get in trouble with the judge, but he ended up in all the business press as being the laughingstock. Don't do that. But here's the thing. We are so worried about these hallucinations. But how many of us know a perfect employee? People make mistakes too. And so the idea is not to expect a perfect answer, maybe, except if your car is driving. But the answer is to get these things to work well and put the right controls in, in case they are wrong, the same thing we do with people. So why do we expect the computers to be better than people in every case? Why don't we just put the right processes in place to account for the fact that these are sometimes not right? The other things, of course, huge training data this thing needs and huge amounts of energy. And so these are other topics we can talk about over time. So the problem is, you got to start with the problem and figure out the right technique. So one way to think about it is there are questions, you can ask. How accurate do I have to be? And what's the cost of being wrong? Getting in a traffic accident or making a wrong medical decision, there's a big cost. Sending the wrong marketing message to somebody, no cost at all. Do you need the answer to be explainable? Because if it does, then those first two are probably useful. Those last two, they're not explainable. How do you do that? Do you need the answers to be the same every time? You're not going to get that with generative AI. And confidentiality-- and confidentiality is less of a problem right now. You can get these generative things that are going to keep you, or at least the vendors promise they will keep you safe. But these are things to think about, right? Then on the other side is the data. Do you have a source of truth, and how true is that data? And number two, is it generalizable? Or are you going to reject all women that apply for your company? So as you're thinking about how to do it, these are questions you can ask about this problem I'm trying to solve right now. And the questions, either you can make the decision or you can ask these questions of your technical people. And first of all, they will now be a little bit afraid of you. But second of all, you will have a better conversation because you are asking these questions. So first bit, what is AI? Four things. Here's how to think about them. Here, if you like traffic lights, here's a nice little chart you can use to think about these things. Where are they good and bad? But that's only part of the problem. That's the part saying, I have a specific problem I want to solve. How do I think about what the right technique is? The real problem is how do I make this work in my organization? So I have more questions for you, maybe some more answers. Are you ready? How do I make it work in the organization? Remember, come back to this technology is not the problem. Transformation is. How do we put the processes, the policies, and the capabilities in place to do this the right way? Because doing it once is hard. But you need to do it over and over, and you need to make it mix in with the rest of the stuff that you do. Here are three challenges to think about when you try to make this stuff work in your organization. And I'd like to say, this is only GenAI, but this is basically anything. How do we work this in? But with generative AI, how do we prioritize what to do and what not to do? What do we do first? What do we do second? And what do we never do? Number two, risk management. What if we are wrong? What if we have a privacy problem? These kinds of things. And last is the capabilities, so four sets of questions you can ask for that. And then after this, I'll have one more little section for you. How do you ensure the safety and the value of what you're doing? And one of the big other ones is learning. How do you not only learn about this innovation, but how do you learn across innovations so you can choose the best way to do things, and you don't end up doing the same thing 10 times? One of the big questions to think about here is, how does your governance process look? And what we've seen in generative AI is multiple approaches, but they tend to fall into top down, this is a very risky, very expensive thing. Let's control everything. And the good thing about that is, we're not going to make mistakes. We're not going to throw money away. We're probably not going to kill a lot of people. But we're also not going to innovate very well because the central part of large organizations, it doesn't always know the best opportunities. The other side is the decentralized way. Hey, go out and innovate. Do whatever you want. Now, here are some rules. Don't steal money. Don't be bad to people. But here are some rules. Innovate within these rules, and tell us about what you're doing. It's a tremendously good way to discover really interesting ideas at the edges. But it's a great way to waste money also. And also, depending on how careful they're being, you can also break some laws when you do that because where the central might try to be very careful, the edges might not. And so what we saw in generative AI is the very top down, safe, but slow, or the very decentralized, very fast, but more risky and more costly. We saw both of those coming out. So at Societe Generale, one of the big French banks, they did it in a very centralized way. But they asked everybody to say, if you want to do this, what would you do? And they got 700 use cases. And what they decided is they did a few of those right away. But the rest they said, wait, because all these cases, an intelligent agent is important. A chatbot to talk to people is important. Programming is important. Let's do this the right way, and we will build everything on top. So they did a few things fast. They told other things to wait until they had these other capabilities set up. They tried to bridge the centralized and decentralized. Sysco that I told you about, they did a different way. They said you know what? This is just another technology. We have a way we think about this. And the first thing we think about is, can we buy this instead of building it? And if we can, we will do that. The second thing they say is, if we think it needs to be programmed, can we do it cheaper and easier with expert systems and statistics? Or do we do the fancy, complicated stuff? And only when it answers all those questions do they do the leading edge, the generative AI. So you see these governance rules, they fit in there. You got to figure out what works with your company, and how does it fit the risk profile that you're thinking about? Some other questions you want to ask, though, are also just as important. Is our culture ready for this? What happens when the computer is just as smart as our expert person? 15 years ago, this started happening in banks, where the computers were as good at judging a high quality or a low quality loan than people were-- or insurance. The computers were just as good at underwriting some things as people. The people felt very threatened by that. And there was a whole process. It's happening in all kinds of jobs. Now, if you've seen the movie Moneyball, have you seen-- I don't know whether-- In America, baseball is a big deal. I don't know if it is here. But there's a big question. How do I tell who is a good potentially new employee for this company? Maybe the computer is better, and people don't like that. So do we have the humility to work with these? Or do we fight against them? Do we have ethics to do the right thing and not the wrong thing? And also in the culture, how good are we at experimenting and trying things and failing fast, rather than trying to have the first answer, the right answer, before we start? The culture's got to be ready for these things. And the way you do that, you have to drive that. You don't just say plug in the model. You got to help people get comfortable, with innovation units, other things. And another one also with people being comfortable, do we have the skills? But what does this mean for careers? A friend of mine, Daniel Rock, looked at GPTs, and he has calculated through a very rigorous process that 46% of all jobs are likely to have 50% of their tasks replaced by AI over time. Now, some jobs, it'll be 100%. These are just-- 46% of jobs will have half of their tasks go. What if you do that job? How do you feel about that? And am I going to-- am I going to go along with this? Or am I going to reject this because I think it's going to hurt my job? So what do you what do you do about this? Certainly, I've done some writing on this. And certainly after lunch, you're going to see some really interesting stuff on that. But AI doesn't have to replace you. How can it make your job easier, reduce your cognitive load? How can it do-- one of the things I do for all the time, I'm a pretty good writer. But I don't do those sexy, creative titles. So I let AI do it now. Give me five potential titles for this. Or I can give it my text and say, make this more exciting. And the other thing we did not expect is the ability to learn with AI. AI is a tremendous teaching tool. And I'm finding I'm learning all the time, just by having it help me think, having it ask questions about what I'm doing. And certainly, I talked about this tutor we are doing. And many places are doing these tutors, including at Cresta and at one of the startups we talked about. So it does not have to replace us. Are you having that conversation with your people about how this-- you're not just saying, we're not going to hurt you because nobody believes that. But can you have the conversation about how we can help you introduce this? So, for example, Dentsu Creative, an advertising firm, that is a firm that you might think should be a little bit nervous about these things. And what they're finding is that these creative people love this. But they're being very systematic in the company about how they introduced this. First of all, they are saying all the boring stuff. Your planning, your proposals, those kinds of things, it will do that for you, take a few words and turn it into a proposal. That's great. What they didn't expect and that they love now is, let's draw a picture. And instead of saying, go away, and in a week, we will have a design for you, now they say, go get a cup of coffee, and in five minutes, we'll have a design for you. So just as if you're talking to people, when you're talking with the computer, be ready to back out of that route and try a different thing. As far as training people for what will the good things be, creativity, working with people, critical thinking. These don't seem to be going out of style. title: Jennifer Tejada CEO of PagerDuty on Leadership, AI, and Digital Transformation
transcript: Speaker: This podcast is brought to you by Knowledge at Wharton. Patti Williams: Jen, it's so nice to have you here. Thank you for coming to the Wharton School, and thank you for our conversation. I'm so, so pleased. Jennifer Tejada: Well, my pleasure. It's great to be back to Wharton. - Awesome. So I thought we would just start and maybe set the ground with, what is PagerDuty, right? So I've read that half of the Fortune 500 and nearly 70 percent of the Fortune 100 use PagerDuty. Tell me a little bit about what PagerDuty is, and what are you doing for these organizations? - Sure. So PagerDuty is a pure software as a service platform that exists to help the largest and most innovative companies in the world deliver reliable and highly available technology services. And if you think about how any business runs that you interact with as a consumer, all of those businesses are running on software and increasingly data and AI today. And the challenge is you become really reliant on the convenience, or the 24 by seven on demand availability of something, and when suddenly your brand experience isn't available to you or doesn't work effectively because of a technology challenge, you don't blame the technology, you blame the brand as a consumer. And so, as the world's been, so to speak, eaten by software and become more technology driven, reliable and available technical infrastructure, software services, applications, and increasingly, LLMs and agents have become mission critical and important. And software, like human beings, is imperfect, and we're also deploying an unprecedented amount of software and technology into the ecosystem, and now new technology in the form of LLMs, agents, applications, integrations, APIs. All that complexity leads to the storming of breakdowns, or what we call incidents. And so the way our customers think about us is we help them manage their digital operations. And increasingly, whether you're a financial services business or online travel and hospitality, a tech company, you know, a ride share platform, all of these platforms increasingly deliver the vast majority of their brand services, their experience, they drive their revenue, driven transactions, all through technology. And so it has to work, and it has to work perfectly all the time. - Yeah, it's amazing. I think for so many organizations, a lot of that was back office, right? It wasn't solution critical. - For sure. - And that's a real change in, I think, the importance of this, and how sort of the center of the strategic sort of value proposition it really is for many of these companies. - Yeah, the way I think about it is you would never think of NASA's mission control as back office, but that is kind of how this works. You have a combination of technology, people, and AI watching how a very complex technology organization operates, and giving you an early read on, you know, where are some things that are looking like they're acting outside of their traditional operating boundaries? Or, where do you see an early sign that something bad is about to happen? And so the goal for us and for our customers is not to just help them respond more effectively when things don't work the way they're supposed to, but to help prevent big issues from happening, and likewise, to learn from every challenge that runs on the platform. And so we've been in the AI business now for almost 16 years. We've been collecting a significant amount of proprietary data since the very beginning of Pager- Duty. We started with machine learning and algorithmic AI, analytical AI, and in the past year and a half, have added generative AI, and just yesterday, announced agentic AI in our platform. - Amazing. We're going to come to that in just a minute. I want to -- you've been at PagerDuty since 2016, I think. -Yeah. - As CEO, right? - That's right. - Eight years is a pretty long time. - It's unusually long for our industry, for sure, particularly for somebody who isn't the original founder. - Yeah, amazing. And I think you took the company public in 2019? - That's right. - As you think about your leadership over those eight years, what are some of the biggest lessons you've learned about leading an organization and leading this organization in particular? - That's a great question. You know, in my early days at Procter & Gamble, in probably some of the first management training that I received there, and they did this tremendous job of putting you through an academy of job specific coursework. And one of the things they would say is, "Act and think like an owner," which goes a little further than, "Spend the company's money like you would your own," right? Some people don't spend their money wisely, right? So that might not actually be a good metaphor. But acting and thinking like an owner isn't just about, you know, trying to drive the share price or the share value up. It's, if you were running this job, or your team like it was your very own business, and that you owned all the investment in, all the outcomes, all the growth, all the challenges, like, how might you think differently? And I think so much about being a CEO, particularly in a culture of innovation, in a high growth startup, in an early public company, is about having that ownership mindset. And in some ways, you know, the company was founded by three co- founders. I sort of became the re-founder or the adoptive parent. And what's interesting about that in the early days, is you're raising that child with the other parents sitting nearby, looking on, right? And so there's a very high standard for how you adapt the company over time, how you develop new capabilities on an existing foundation, how you drive disruption, even when you may be attacking somebody's sacred cows, so to speak. And probably the most exciting thing for me has been how you first to reinvent yourself. We've been through many chapters and many transitions as a company. We were very small. You know, 30 million in ARR when I joined, less than 200 people. And now we're over 1,000 people, and close to a half a billion in ARR. And so -- and we went from being this private, you know, series A backed startup, to being a public company traded on the New York Stock Exchange for now almost six years. And so through all those chapters as a leader, it's never boring, right? You're always having to anticipate, like, what does the next leg of the journey look like? How do we need to be prepared for that? And as you get bigger, those preparation cycles take longer. You need to be further out in front of kind of what's coming. And one of the things I'm really proud of is, we did, I think, quite a good job of future proofing our platform for big data, for AI and machine learning, and now generative. We rallied around one of our core value propositions, which is trust. So you know, PagerDuty's core reliability engineering is critically important, because if we have to be up when the rest of the world is down, and our customers hold us to a much higher standard than most technology and SaaS platforms. And so in the 16 years of the company's existence, we've never had a maintenance window. A maintenance window is when you log on to something and it says, "Sorry, we're not available. We'll be right back." Can you imagine if you were undergoing a major technology incident, a ransomware attack here at Wharton, and the one platform that is supposed to help you detect that and manage it and resolve it and remediate is like not available for that hour? So that -- our ability to keep innovating and expanding our product set and our platform, while at the same time, delivering the level of fidelity and reliability and trust that our customers, some of the most -- I think, like most critical and highest standard holding customers out there in the marketplace, to live up to that ongoing standard, as the bar keeps getting higher because the technology gets more complex, has been a really big challenge. And we've done it while delivering very high gross margins, while continuing to grow, and, you know, while becoming a profitable company and a company that produces a lot of cash flow. - Amazing. One of the things that I think is particularly interesting is that you don't have a typical tech CEO background. - No. - Could you talk a little bit about your background, how you got here, and how do you think that makes you a better adoptive parent? - Yeah. Well, I grew up in small towns across the Midwest. I went to the University of Michigan on a scholarship. I got a liberal arts degree in organizational behavior and business management, which was basically psych for groups, you know, is the way I would think about it. And going to a big university like Michigan or like Penn, one of the benefits is you don't just learn how to learn, you learn how to navigate a complex system, and you learn how to advocate when you're, you know, a small speck in a really big universe. And I felt like my experience at Michigan prepared me for the world in a lot of ways, coming out of a, you know, smaller city, into this very diverse environment where I had to fight for classes, I had to kind of choose my own major, and at the time, like I was a 19 year old kid that felt very stressful. But when I look back on it, like the opportunity to choose my own adventure and just spend four years just discovering what was interesting to me, what I thought was going to be important in the world, like that was a very strong foundation. And I didn't really know what I wanted to be when I grew up. I still am trying to figure it out actually. I was originally going to go into healthcare administration, and the industry was deregulating at the time, so I decided to just go to work for a couple of years and learn how to adult and just get some experience under my belt, and by the grace of God, got a job with Procter & Gamble, and they had this phenomenal leadership rotation. So from the very early days of my career, I had -- I was taught, I think, important basics and foundations of what makes a great leader. How to find your own leadership voice, how to think about how to surround yourself with the kinds of other leaders or people that have skills that complement your skills and experience. And so as early as in my very early twenties, I was already thinking about, how do you compose a great team? You know, what makes the collective of a team better than just the sum of the individuals? So some of those really early lessons stuck with me for a long time. But when I -- you know, I showed up in the tech industry in the mid to late '90s, because it was moving fast. I could see this innovation happening, and I -- not only did I not want to be left behind, I didn't want to be a simple participant. I wanted to be a part of leading, you know, that -- leading that disruption and that innovation from the front. And so I took a very big risk and went to work for a supply chain automation software company called ITU, and I leveraged what I learned at Procter & Gamble and what Procter & Gamble was known for, which was brand and marketing and go to market, and to some extent product, because product management at P&G is really brand, and kind of leveraged that to get my first job in tech. And I didn't send out any resumes, I met a guy on an airplane. And so, you know, I always remind my daughter, who's a college sophomore right now, like, "You've always got to be ready to give your elevator pitch." And sometimes you're only going up two floors, right? Sometimes you might have the Sears Tower to work with. But when someone asks you who you are and what you do, like, make sure you put your best foot forward in an authentic way that makes someone want to learn more. And I think that liberal arts degree, I think having an undergraduate education was really all about identifying complex problems and figuring out how to pick them apart, but then make the solution accessible to lots of different kinds of people, prepared me really well for general management, right? And then I'd also say, I come from like a really hard working family, so I have a sick work ethic, sick in a good way. And I also came from a family that really expects you to contribute to your community and to not wait to be asked. To take initiative, to think about how you serve the community around you. And I think that mindset of like looking out into the community and figuring out where you can add value is really important in the CEO job right now, because we have such a diverse stakeholder community now, much more so than even five years or 10 years ago in the role. - That's really interesting. So you know, as a marketing professor, one of the things that I have appreciated, besides the fact that you came from a marketing background at P&G, and you have this sort of branding mindset that you bring, that I've heard you say that you spend about half of your time with your customers. - I do. - I'm not sure most CEOs, even in marketing driven organizations, spend half of their time with their customers. Talk a little bit about why you do that, how you think it gives you advantages as a leader. - Yeah, I mean, part of it was just choosing a perspective that enabled me to devote time to sort of understanding our users, but also the economic buyer, the CEO the CFO, the CIO, who makes a decision to sign a multi- million dollar, multi-year agreement with us. I mean, that is a long term material partnership for a lot of the companies we serve, and they have lots of choices. And so part of it was figuring out how to get inside the minds of both our users and our buyers, and really understand what was important in their business. Because I think it's easy to become sort of tunnel vision about like what your product does, and focusing purely around the use cases that your products support. And that's how you miss pivots. That's how you miss opportunities to move into adjacent areas. It's more how our customers' jobs are evolving. Like, what is keeping them up late at night? And I mean, what are the big problems that they worry about, not for this week or for this month or for Friday's payroll, but like, what are the big problems that are keeping them up 18 months from now, three years from now, five years from now? And what's getting in the way of them positioning themselves and their businesses for success? And can you be part of moving those obstacles out of the way, or addressing those obstacles, or even changing the way the company operates? And so digital transformation has been like a playground. You know, somebody said that, "If you love what you do, you never work a day in your life." And I mean, I really -- I love the study of different businesses. I get to look at businesses across industry and find patterns in terms of where there are some common challenges or common threads, where there are emerging threats or opportunities, and use that pattern recognition to inform our product roadmap, to think about the pace and speed with which we invest in innovation, and where we might decide to say no to something. And I feel like my ability to anticipate what's coming really comes through the the sum of all the conversations I have with our customers and our prospects. And it also helped me approach networking. Like, I've never been somebody who likes to network. I don't like to just go to a thing and stand at the cocktail table with my name tag on and meet people. But when I shaped it in the perspective of, this is my market research, and you know, these are people that need to be part of my community that informs how we allocate capital, how we think about our future roadmap, how we even think about our vision and mission as a company, it made it not feel so much like networking, and made it a much more, I think, tactical learning pursuit that delivers a really strategic outcome in the end. And it's funny, because I think a lot of people in the industry have given me feedback that I have a really strong, deep and wide network, and I always giggle inside when someone says that to me, because I don't like networking. I don't really love going to conferences. I'm really picky about, like, which events I'll attend and who I'm going to invest my time speaking with, and what I'm trying to learn. Like, what are my goals in that hour and a half, or the 16 minutes I'm going to have with that person? Is there one thing I want to try and take away from that? But the thing that surprised me the most is just how much pattern recognition emerges, and how helpful that can be. In the early days, when we were really an amazing app that developers loved to use themselves, I could see this pattern around, you know, data pattern recognition, like being able to action analytical insights very quickly when time really mattered. So you know, if you're a trading platform in the financial services industry, and you somehow can't manage transactions, because your transaction environment goes down, like, not only are you losing significant money every second, but you're also in the risk of, you know, compliance breach, regulatory issues, fines, even, you know, being prevented from continuing to operate in certain jurisdictions, and that can happen in minutes. And so the need to move fast really matters. And so, you know, as I've gotten to know my customers, I've also gotten to -- been able to identify patterns in certain verticals, new use cases that I see that are common across a vertical, and that usually comes from talking to the CIO, the CTO, the CEO, not the user. Like, not somebody who is is down, you know, hands on keys, so to speak, phone in hand, using your actual application. I think that's sometimes hard for people to distinguish, right? - Yeah, absolutely. I mean, so first of all, as a professor, I think we love people who love to learn, and it sounds like you're bringing that growth mindset to the -- you know, to the experience of networking, but also to thinking about how you're leading your organization, so that's amazing. I wonder if you can tell me a little bit about some of that pattern recognition as we're thinking about AI. You know, you've been in the space. The company's been in the space for a while. But for many organizations, it's maybe a year old. They are just trying to figure out something that moves so fast it's hard to keep up with, figure out what the use cases are. And you know, here at Wharton, we're really lucky, we have this base of faculty who have been in the space for a long period of time, and so we're able to share our expertise. But I think, what does it look like to -- what are the kinds of patterns you see across organizations when it comes to understanding and using AI? - Yeah, I mean, I think things often happen in stages or phases. And you know, what I initially saw was a very big hype cycle. Like, a lot of our large enterprise customers, knowing that AI was a thing, recognizing quickly that it was going to be important and disruptive, but then falling into one -- well, two camps, or in some cases, both. This fear of missing out. Like, I need to be doing something, my board is demanding I do something, I must do something. Like, we have to do something. We have to get started, or start starting. And then also this fear of getting in. Oh my gosh, this is scary. This could be really dangerous. You know, we could ruin our brand reputationally by doing the wrong thing and not knowing, like, how to start and how to start in a safe way. And the challenge when you're going through a disruptive phase or a disruptive cycle in the technical industry is, if you -- it's very easy to use risk as an excuse to innovate gradually or incrementally, and generally, more slowly than the disruptive players that have a, you know, stronger risk profile and are willing to make bigger bets, right? And that is often how, you know, captains of industry can be left behind, right? And we've seen this prior to AI. We've seen this in like the payments space, for instance. Who would have thought that like our children would not have cash and would use things like Venmo and CashApp, you know? When we think about just how that particular sub segment has disrupted traditional financial services and their access to consumer assets, right? Like, it's just a pretty interesting example, where those startup payments companies had nothing to lose, right? And the incumbents are trying to protect, you know, their current incumbency, but also figure out how to move faster and do things that are a little scary. title: Leadership in the Era of Digital Transformation | Prof. Alex Siow | TEDxYouth@RafflesInstitution
transcript: The New Oxford Dictionary defines leadership as the action of leading a group of people or an organization, and the Collins Dictionary defines the leadership as the qualities that make someone a good leader. All the methods a leader uses to do his or her job. But, what is the right definition? Everyone's understanding of the word could be very different. And mainly because of the experience each of us has gone through. And that our opinion of what leadership is is different from another person's. My belief is that leadership is everything that has been defined and yet more. I also believe that leadership is situational. And different situations require specific kinds of leadership. Now, generally for leadership to happen, there must be someone who is leading and others who are following. But, why would people follow a leader? What characteristics must the leader possess? I put down some characteristics which I think are important. First, the leader has to be visionary. He must be able to articulate a vision so that people can identify with him. So, he must be an outstanding individual. He cannot just be a run-of-the-mill person. And he must share a common goal with his followers so that they can bond with him to achieve the common goal. I believe he should have a commanding personality as well, so that he can command the respect of his followers. And he must have a good stature and good reputation. I'm sure with people will not follow a leader with a bad reputation. Right? And the leader has a capability to do what most people cannot. And for that reason, the followers know that if they follow the leader, the chances of them achieving their goals is much greater. And so uh instead of doing themselves, they'd rather follow the leader. There are other personal attributes of a leader that will include honesty, integrity, sincerity, and openness. The leader has to play various roles when leading his team, which includes being a communicator, an educator, a motivator, and he is also a politician. As a As the leader, he networks with uh other leaders and shield the followers from the politics in the organization so that they can devote themselves to the task rather than playing politics. He's also a relationship builder to build relationship amongst the team. And also with external parties. And last but not least, he's a change manager. The followers will have to face a number of challenges as they progress. And because of the changing circumstances and changing environments. The leader helps the team to cope with changes that come their way. Now, on top of all these skills, when we talk about the business leader, the business leader today will require additional skills. Firstly, a strong business perspective about how the economy is doing and how the business should adjust to that environment. And because information technology is so important to businesses today, he has to be continuously informed on developments in IT and interpret their significance to the business. He has to manage the teams so that they are change-oriented according to the environment changes and a catalyst to business thinking. Let us now take a look at the current era of transformation and more specifically at digital transformation, which is the topic which I would like to cover today and it is a password in the industry. Digital transformation happens because businesses need to overcome digital disruption. Firstly, why are there disruptions? There will always be disruptions because the human race is always innovating. And you will innovate, there will be new changes, new technology, there will be disruption. The current wave of disruption is because of the rapid advancement uh technology. Human beings innovate in order to ensure their survival. They will employ whatever is the latest technology that will ensure their survival. The mankind innovate because they are continuously trying to achieve a higher standard of living. Everyone hopes their life will be better tomorrow for themselves and for the future generations. So therefore, there will be no end to disruption. So we can forget about it. All right, if you think that disruption will end. As is commonly said, the only constant in business is change. If we do not change, then unfortunately, we will be left behind. So how do we prepare for disruption since we cannot avoid it? First, we need to have awareness of the emerging technologies that are coming to disrupt our business. We need to maintain our agility and be prepared to change. We need to get out of our comfort zone so that we do not rely on age-old business practices and processes that are becoming obsolete. A lot of people stay in their comfort zone because they feel safe and the environment is familiar. Not knowing that the comfort zone will lead them actually to the downfall. We have to pick up new knowledge and skills and be aware of signs of impending change. In the new millennium, the advent of new technologies has made this very challenging. New business models enabled by technology will emerge to topple traditional business thinking. Technology like the internet, big data analytics, AI, machine learning, internet of things, 6G networks, etc. have been effectively employed by emerging business leaders to challenge incumbents in the marketplace and even usurp their leadership positions. A new leadership model based on agility and an agile mindset is needed in the era of transformation. So, we call this agility, digital agility. Digital agility describes the ease with which an organization can rapidly enable, update, change, or adapt their processes to the changes in the business environment. Why is then an agile mindset important? Firstly, we live in a VUCA world. If you have not heard this word before, it stands for volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity. Rapid advances in technology has brought about digital disruption as we have examined in the recent few years. The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated business disruption and has created a new normal for work. Work has shifted from the office to the home. And even after the pandemic is largely over, people are reluctant to go back to the office. The big changes in the business environment means that business must be able to be agile to adjust to the changes. Let's look at the principles of agile digital transformation. It starts with a transformative vision. A vision is like a call to action. It describes what the business aims to achieve and how the future will look like. There must be a strong focus on building digital customer engagement. We need to put the customer in the center of our business and use the latest technologies to engage with customers. And give them an excellent customer experience when they are interacting with us. If we do not give customer the right attention, they will move on to our competitors. Right, that's the reality of business today. Next, we have to support the vision with risk management and security management. We have to manage the risks that come along with new technology. And believe you me, all new technologies carries risk with them. And with so much data that we collect, we have to ensure our systems are secure and we guard our data, especially customer data, extremely well so that the customer have confidence to do business with us. From all the data we have collected when doing business, we should endeavor to derive insights using data visualization tools. Insight about the customers, about the environment, and about the competitors. Finally, we need to embrace digital agility to create advantage for the company by responding quickly to changes in technology, to the marketplace, and to the business environment. In summary, leading digital transformation begins with the agile mindset. And the agile mindset helps the organization to be able to adjust business processes to fit the changing business landscape. Customer centricity is important as the changing business landscape is brought about by changes in customer demands and preferences. Digital leadership is important to overcome the current digital disruption. And it is the strategic use of technology and innovation to achieve the business goals. To conclude, leadership is indeed situational as we said right in the beginning. Face of massive disruption in business, many companies have to reinvent themselves or perish. Indeed, many traditional leaders in business have gone out of business or have lost their leadership position in the marketplace. In the era of digital transformation, those who seek to be leaders must be prepared to get out of the comfort zones and make decisive changes to their business models to meet the challenges posed by emerging technologies. The challenges will only get more intense because the speed of change will continue to be excel to accelerate and to be more intense. And with that, I thank you for your attention.
